title: Round 6: Explain a distributed transaction and failure recovery strategy
description: Explain how to keep data consistent across multiple services when a single database transaction is no longer an option.

data.text: When an operation spans multiple databases or services, a traditional ACID transaction no longer works. The interviewer wants to know whether you understand the trade-offs and can choose a pattern that matches the business risk.

Two-phase commit coordinates a decision across systems, but it blocks during the prepare phase and creates availability problems. If the coordinator crashes after some systems have prepared, those systems remain locked until the coordinator recovers. In modern distributed systems, availability is often valued more than strict consistency.

terms.definition: Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability: the guarantees a traditional database transaction provides.
A protocol where a coordinator first asks all participants to prepare, then instructs them to commit or roll back.
A sequence of local transactions where each step has a compensating action to undo its effect if a later step fails.
The property that applying the same operation multiple times has the same effect as applying it once.
A consistency model where updates propagate asynchronously and all replicas converge to the same state over time.

data.title: Saga pattern for an order
data.content: A saga breaks a global transaction into local transactions with compensating actions:
data.code:
1. Order Service creates order in Pending state
2. Saga sends ReserveInventory command
3. Inventory Service reserves items, emits InventoryReserved
4. Saga sends ChargePayment command
5. Payment Service charges card, emits PaymentCharged
6. Saga sends ConfirmOrder command
7. Order Service marks order Confirmed

If step 5 fails:
- Payment Service emits PaymentFailed
- Saga sends CompensateInventory command
- Inventory Service releases the reservation

rows: Legacy systems with a single operator
Complex workflows needing a central tracker
Transient failures with safe retry semantics

items: Store saga state in a durable table so you can resume after a crash.
Make every command idempotent by including a unique saga ID and step number.
Use a dead-letter queue for commands that fail after all retries.
Run a periodic reconciliation job that compares the saga state with downstream systems and fixes drift.
Alert on sagas that stay in a Pending or Compensating state for longer than the SLA.
Use circuit breakers to prevent cascading failures when a downstream service is down.

data.caption: Saga orchestration flow with compensating actions on failure
data.definition:
graph TD
    A[Start Saga] --> B[Step 1: Create Order]
    B --> C{Step 1 ok?}
    C -->|No| X[Abort Saga]
    C -->|Yes| D[Step 2: Reserve Inventory]
    D --> E{Step 2 ok?}
    E -->|No| Y[Compensate: Cancel Order]
    E -->|Yes| F[Step 3: Charge Payment]
    F --> G{Step 3 ok?}
    G -->|No| Z[Compensate: Release Inventory]
    G -->|Yes| H[Step 4: Confirm Order]
    H --> I[Saga Complete]
    Z --> Y
    Y --> X

data.title: Design for failure, not for success
data.text: When you explain a distributed transaction, spend more time on what happens when a service is down than on the happy path. Interviewers are testing whether you have seen failures in production and whether you built systems that can recover gracefully.

Event sourcing stores every state change as an immutable event. Instead of compensating a failed transaction, you replay events to rebuild the current state. This eliminates the need for compensating transactions but requires a different mental model and tooling.

cards.title: Choreography
cards.description: Services react to events from other services with no central coordinator.

cards.title: Orchestration
cards.description: A central saga orchestrator tells each service what to do and when.

cards.title: Event sourcing
cards.description: Store every state change as an immutable event; rebuild state by replaying.
pros: Temporal queries: what was the state at time T?
cons: Requires snapshots for large event streams

items.question: When should I use two-phase commit instead of a saga?
items.answer: Only when you need strong consistency and can tolerate reduced availability, such as financial transfers within a single data center owned by one operator.

items.question: How do I handle duplicate messages in a saga?
items.answer: Make every step idempotent by storing the saga ID and step number. Before processing, check whether the step has already completed.

items.question: What happens if the saga orchestrator crashes?
items.answer: The orchestrator should store its state durably. On restart, it reads the saga state table, finds the last successful step, and resumes or compensates from there.

items.question: Can I use a saga for read operations?
items.answer: Sagas are best for write workflows. For reads, use event sourcing or materialized views with eventual consistency instead.

data.title: Summary
points: Prefer eventual consistency with compensating actions over two-phase commit
Make every operation idempotent so retries are safe
Use orchestration when the workflow is complex, choreography when services are loosely coupled
Store the saga state so you can resume or compensate after a crash
data.takeaway: Consistency is a spectrum. The right pattern depends on your business tolerance for temporary inconsistency and your team's ability to operate the solution.
